# Introduction

This tutorial collects the most frequent errors found in the course exercises. Most of them come from a few basic ideas. If you get these right, your scripts will be much more reliable.

Run the code yourself as you read. Some chunks are **meant to fail**: they show the error so that you can recognise it when it happens in your own scripts.

# Creating a result is not the same as saving it

This is the most common mistake. If you don't use `<-`, R only **prints** the result in the console. Nothing is stored, and the original object stays the same.

```{r}
months <- c("Jan", NA, "Feb", "Mar")

# Wrong: the result is printed, but months still contains NA
months[!is.na(months)]
factor(months)
months
class(months)            # still "character"

# Right: assign the result
months <- months[!is.na(months)]
months <- factor(months)
months
class(months)            # "factor"
```

The same applies to importing data and creating data frames:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
read.csv("iris.csv")                       # Wrong: printed and lost
iris_data <- read.csv("iris.csv")          # Right

data.frame(site, x, y)                     # Wrong: printed and lost
df_exercise <- data.frame                  # Wrong: this stores the *function*, not your table
df_exercise <- data.frame(site, x, y)      # Right
```

> **Rule:** if you want to keep it, assign it with `<-`.

# Data types change silently (coercion)

A vector can only hold **one type** of data. If you add an element of a different type, R converts the whole vector without warning.

## Integers need an `L`

```{r}
x <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)
class(x)

x[5] <- 10      # 10 is a double (numeric)...
x               # position 4 is filled with NA
class(x)        # ...so x is now "numeric"

x <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)
x[5] <- 10L     # 10L is an integer
class(x)        # still "integer"
```

Watch out:

| Code                | Class   |
|---------------------|---------|
| `c(1, 2, 3)`        | numeric |
| `seq(3, 7, by = 2)` | numeric |
| `c(1L, 2L, 3L)`     | integer |
| `1:3`               | integer |

## Adding text turns everything into text

```{r}
y <- c(4L, 5L, 6L)
y[5] <- "five"
y
class(y)
```

## Why does this happen?

Think of the data types as a ladder, from the most specific to the most general:

**logical → integer → numeric → character**

Each step can represent everything in the steps below it:

- a logical can become an integer (`TRUE` is `1`, `FALSE` is `0`);
- an integer can become a number (`3L` is `3.0`);
- anything can become text (`"3"`, `"TRUE"`).

But not the other way round: `2.5` cannot be an integer without losing the decimal, and `"five"` cannot be a number.

So R converts all elements to the most **general** type present, so that no value is lost:

```{r}
c(TRUE, 2L)       # integer (TRUE becomes 1)
c(1L, 2.5)        # numeric
c(3L, "five")     # character
c(TRUE, "a")      # character
```

Once a vector has become text, you can no longer calculate with it:

```{r, warning = TRUE}
mean(y)
```

This often happens when importing data: a single cell with text (such as `"n.d."` or `"<5"`) turns the whole column into character.

```{r}
counts <- c("12", "8", "<5", "20")   # as it would arrive from a CSV
class(counts)
```

> **Rule:** after changing a vector, check it with `class()`.

# Choosing the right way to save

| You want to...                                     | Use                                              | File     |
|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|----------|
| Share a table with Excel or other software         | `write.csv(obj, "file.csv", row.names = FALSE)`  | `.csv`   |
| Save **one or several** R objects                  | `save(obj1, obj2, file = "file.RData")`          | `.RData` |
| Save **one** R object (and load it with any name)  | `saveRDS(obj, "file.rds")`                       | `.rds`   |
| Save **everything** in your environment            | `save.image("file.RData")`                       | `.RData` |

## Before saving: load the data and prepare the folder

The examples below use the `BCI` dataset, which comes with the **vegan** package. `BCI` does not exist in your session until you install the package (once), load it (every session) and load the dataset:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("vegan")   # only once, if you don't have it yet
library(vegan)
data(BCI)
```

If you skip this, every line that uses `BCI` will fail with `object 'BCI' not found`.

**Watch out:** in these examples we save the files **inside a `data/` subfolder**. `save()`, `saveRDS()` and `write.csv()` create files, but they **do not create folders**. If `data/` does not exist, you get an error that gives no clue about the real problem:

```{r, error = TRUE}
save(iris, file = "folder_that_does_not_exist/iris.RData")
```

So check first whether the folder exists, and create it only if it doesn't:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dir.exists("data")              # TRUE or FALSE

if (!dir.exists("data")) {
  dir.create("data")
}
```

We come back to folders and paths in the section [Working directory, projects and paths](#working-directory-projects-and-paths).

## Common errors

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Saves the whole environment, not just BCI
save.image(file = "data/BCI.RData")

# Better
save(BCI, file = "data/BCI.RData")

# This is NOT a CSV file: it is an RData file with a .csv name
save(BCI, file = "data/BCI.csv")

# Right
write.csv(BCI, "data/BCI.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## The mysterious column "X"

By default, `write.csv()` also writes the row names. When you import the file again, they appear as an extra column called `X`.

```{r}
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")   # a temporary file, so we don't clutter your folder

write.csv(iris, tmp)                       # adds row names
names(read.csv(tmp))

write.csv(iris, tmp, row.names = FALSE)    # Right
names(read.csv(tmp))
```

# Deleting objects: be precise

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rm(x)                 # deletes x
rm(x, y, site)        # deletes these three objects
rm(list = ls())       # deletes EVERYTHING in the environment
```

Read the task carefully. If it asks you to "delete the vectors", use `rm(x, y, site)`, not `rm(list = ls())`, or your data frame will be deleted too.

Also remember that you can only remove objects that exist. If you create `site` *inside* `data.frame()`, there is no `site` object to remove:

```{r, error = TRUE}
df_test <- data.frame(site = c("A", "B"), value = c(1, 2))
rm(site)
```

> **Rule:** run `ls()` before and after `rm()` to see what you deleted.

# Working directory, projects and paths

- **Use RStudio projects.** When you open a project, the working directory is set automatically to the project folder.
- **Avoid `setwd()` with absolute paths** such as `setwd("C:/Users/myname/Desktop/...")`. Your script will only work on your computer.
- **Use relative paths** from the project folder:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
getwd()                        # where am I?
list.files()                   # what's here?
dir.create("data")             # create a subfolder
iris_data <- read.csv("data/iris.csv")
```

When you write only `"iris.csv"`, you are saying "I am reading or saving this file **directly in the working directory**". When you write `"data/iris.csv"`, you are saying "I am reading or saving this file **in the `data` subfolder of the working directory**".

# Data frames: all columns must have the same length

```{r, error = TRUE}
x <- c(1L, 2L, 3L, NA, 5L)                 # length 5
site <- c("A", "B", "C")                   # length 3
data.frame(site, x)
```

```{r}
site <- c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E")         # length 5
df_exercise <- data.frame(site, x)         # works
df_exercise
```

> **Rule:** check with `length()` before building a data frame.

# Ordered factors need explicit levels

When we saw factors in the previous tutorial, we did not work with **ordered** factors. Here is an example, because they will be useful later in the course.

Without `levels`, R sorts factor levels **alphabetically**:

```{r}
months <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr")
levels(factor(months))
```

Writing the levels alphabetically yourself has the same problem. For months, give the chronological order:

```{r}
months <- factor(months,
                 levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                            "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"),
                 ordered = TRUE)
months
```

Level names must match the data exactly: `"jan"` is not `"Jan"`, and any value without a matching level becomes `NA`:

```{r}
factor(c("Jan", "jan", "Feb"), levels = c("Jan", "Feb"))
```

# Functions that are easy to confuse

| Function                    | What it does                                                |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `install.packages("vegan")` | Downloads and installs a package (once)                     |
| `library(vegan)`            | Loads it into your session (every session)                  |
| `data(BCI)`                 | Loads a dataset that comes with R or a package              |
| `str(BCI)`                  | Shows the **structure** of an object                        |
| `structure()`               | Something else: it sets attributes. Not for inspecting data |
| `head()`                    | Shows the first **6** rows by default                       |

Also remember:

- **R is case-sensitive:** `Library(vegan)` gives an error; `library(vegan)` works.
- **No package is needed for CSV files:** `read.csv()` and `write.csv()` are part of base R.
- **Dependencies load automatically:** `library(vegan)` already loads `permute`.

```{r, error = TRUE}
Library(stats)
```

# Keep your script clean: tips for working on the exercises

A script you hand in should run from top to bottom without errors and contain only what is needed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Exercise 3 - Your Name
# Date

# 1. Create integer vectors
x <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)
y <- c(4L, 5L, 6L)
class(x)

# 2. ...
```

- One comment per step, matching the task.
- Don't mix tutorial code with exercise code.
- Remove duplicated blocks and failed attempts.
- Make sure each comment describes what the code really does.
- Before handing it in: **restart R** (*Session → Restart R*) and run the whole script. If it works, it's ready.

## Good practices and clean code

Writing clean code is not only about the exercises: it makes your scripts easier to read for others, and for yourself in a few months. A few habits worth adopting from the start:

- Use clear, consistent object names (`tree_height`, not `th2` or `x_final_final`).
- Put spaces around `<-`, `=` and operators, and after commas: `x <- c(1, 2, 3)`.
- Keep lines short and break long function calls over several lines.
- Write comments that explain *why* you do something, not only *what*.
- Load all packages at the top of the script.

If you want to go further:

- Wickham, H. *The tidyverse style guide*. <https://style.tidyverse.org/>. The most widely used style conventions for R code.
- Wilson, G., Bryan, J., Cranston, K., Kitzes, J., Nederbragt, L. & Teal, T. K. (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. *PLoS Computational Biology*, 13(6), e1005510. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510>. Practical advice on organising data, code and projects in research.

# The golden habit: check every step

The students who checked their results after each step made the fewest mistakes.

| Check                         | Function                   |
|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
| What type is it?              | `class()`                  |
| How long is it?               | `length()`                 |
| How many rows and columns?    | `dim()`                    |
| What does it look like?       | `head()`, `str()`          |
| What is in my environment?    | `ls()`                     |
| Where am I working?           | `getwd()`, `list.files()`  |

If you don't check, you're guessing.
